title: Weather App
summary: Serve current weather, forecasts and history from locally stored readings refreshed on a schedule per location cell.
narrative:
A weather widget should show current conditions, an hourly and 7-day forecast, and a history chart for any location. Build the API version: the Third-Party API is an outside weather provider. Snap locations to roughly 10 km grid cells and register a cell for scheduled polling the first time someone requests it. A new cell can show a loading state until its first reading arrives; users never trigger a provider call on the request path.

Expect 10 M daily active users opening the app about 5 times each: ~50 M requests/day, or ~600 requests/s, with ~3 K/s at breakfast peaks. Poll ~50 K active cells every 15 minutes: 50 K / 900 ≈ 55 provider calls/s. At ~200 B per reading, 50 K × 96 readings/day × 200 B ≈ 1 GB/day of history. Spread polling across the interval to respect provider quotas.

Clients reach redundant Web Servers through a CDN and Load Balancer. Refresh the open widget every few minutes and show observation timestamps. Cache forecast responses per cell at the CDN for a few minutes; Web Servers read latest conditions and forecasts from Cache and history from the Time-Series Database. Register new cells with the Task Scheduler, which dispatches redundant Workers to pull the provider, append readings and refresh Cache. Optionally archive raw payloads in Blob Storage for backfill and replay, and add Monitoring for stale cells and provider errors.

functional: Show current conditions, hourly and 7-day forecasts, and a history chart by location
Snap locations to ~10 km cells and register newly requested cells for scheduled polling
Poll the provider every 15 minutes via Workers; append readings to the Time-Series Database and refresh latest conditions and forecasts in Cache
Serve cached responses through the CDN for minutes; refresh the open widget every few minutes, show observation timestamps and show a loading state for a cell awaiting its first poll
nonFunctional: Handle ~600 requests/s on average and ~3 K/s at peak without user-driven provider calls
Keep collection available after one Worker failure and reads available after one Web Server failure
Measure freshness by cell and expose the observation timestamp
constraints: Never connect the Web Server directly to the Third-Party API; requests read our own stores
Clients must not read the Time-Series Database directly
Connect the Task Scheduler to Workers and stagger polls within provider quotas
capacity: 10 M DAU × ~5 opens/day ≈ 50 M requests/day ≈ 600/s; ~3 K/s peak
~50 K active cells / 900 s ≈ 55 provider calls/s
~50 K cells × 96 readings/day × ~200 B ≈ 1 GB/day of history
specs.tradeoff: Scheduled API polling trades minute-level staleness for predictable provider load and reusable cached forecasts. In the sensor version, sensors push readings into a Message Queue and Stream Processor instead of polling the provider; the latest-value Cache and history store stay the same.
specs.bonus: Connect Workers to Blob Storage to archive raw provider payloads for replay and add Monitoring for provider failures and stale cells.

topologyRules.message: Never call the weather provider on the request path — serve from your own stores; the provider is rate-limited and slow
Clients read weather history through the Web Server, never directly from the Time-Series Database.

resilienceRules.message: Run at least two Web Servers so weather reads survive one failure.
Run at least two Workers so one failure does not stop weather collection.
Connect the Task Scheduler to Workers that perform provider polling.

hints: Start with Client → CDN → Load Balancer → Web Server. Read current weather and forecasts from Cache, and charts from the Time-Series Database. Keep provider calls off this request path.

Connect Web Server → Task Scheduler to register cells, then Task Scheduler → Worker → Third-Party API. Workers also write Time-Series Database and Cache; stagger the ~55 polls/s rather than polling every cell simultaneously.

Run two Web Servers and two Workers. Connect each Web Server to Cache, Time-Series Database and Task Scheduler; the scheduler reaches both Workers, each pulling the provider and writing both stores. Add Worker → Blob Storage and Web Server → Monitoring.
tips: How is data ingested - there are two versions of this question: via an API, and via sensors.
